newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Co-op defends age-old mutual tradition.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Co-op defends age-old mutual tradition.

text.p: Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society, which on Thursday succeeded in scotching a bitter takeover attempt, has its origins in the Industrial Revolution.

One of 51 separate co-operative societies in Britain, it was founded in 1863 to serve the needs of consumer co-operatives but traces its origins to 1844 when a group called the "Rochdale Pioneers" banded together in Lancashire, north west England.
The Manchester-based mutually-owned group now supplies most of Britain's co-operative retail societies with everything from babyfood to coffins, truly encapsulating the idea of "cradle to grave".

The Rochdale Pioneers, a group of artisans including cloggers, tailors and hawkers, are regarded as the founding fathers of the worldwide co-operative movement. They set up their first retail shop in Rochdale's Toad Lane in 1844.
Their aim was to sell pure, unadulterated food to working people at a time when most food was heavily adulterated and was not weighed properly.

These ideas spread as quickly as the Industrial Revolution itself and the co-operative movement is now represented in more than 100 countries around the world, with an estimated membership in the region of 700 million individuals.
The CWS now has diverse businesses ranging from supermarkets and funeral parlours to travel agents, an insurance company and the ethically and environmentally driven but profitable Co-op Bank.

In June 1996 it had 665 food shops, 56 non-food shops, 241 travel agencies, 346 funeral parlours, 56 opticians, 18 garages, 11 dairies, creameries and factories and 50,000 acres of farmland, making it Britain's biggest commercial farmer.
It also has bank branches and insurance outlets through its subsidiaries.

A Co-op insider said the international importance of the Rochdale Pioneers is reflected by the fact that many of the visitors to Toad Lane, now a museum, are from overseas, with a large number from the U.S. and Japan.
The Pioneers were themselves inspired by social reformer Robert Owen who started an industrial career in Manchester in 1786, managing a number of mills and a wholesale business.

Owen developed what today's CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth described in a history of the organisation as a "passionate concern about the consequences for working men and women of the Industrial Revolution" and formed his ideas on a new form of society.
The first Co-operative Congress, attended by Owen, was held in Manchester in 1831 and resolutions were put forward on the need for wholesale trading companies.

Early co-ops were founded on the principles of one man, one vote, a distributable surplus or dividend on purchases -- known as the "divi", a fixed return on capital, protection for the consumer and a membership open to all.
The CWS, which employees 35,000 people and has a turnover -- excluding its banking and insurance interests -- of more than three billion pounds ($4.9 billion), has a complex membership structure.

Its board is elected by retail co-operative society shareholders and CWS retail branches. The number of directors eligible to be elected from each of four geographical sections depends on the total purchases from the CWS within each section.
This has until now been an obstacle to takeover. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
